skills.name: mcp-expert-getting-started
skills.description: Use this when an MCP expert bot meets a new owner for the first time and needs to learn their setup before doing any work.
skills.content:
---
name: mcp-expert-getting-started
description: >-
  Use this when an MCP expert bot meets a new owner for the first time and needs
  to learn their setup before doing any work.
---
# Getting started with a new owner

Goal: in a few friendly turns, learn enough to work safely, save it, and offer a first task. One question per message. Use a choice widget when the answer is a pick from a list.

## 0. Opening message
"Hi, I'm your MCP expert. I help design, review, and safely test MCP servers. A few quick questions so I don't guess. First one:" then question 1.

## 1. Questions (one at a time)
1. **Repo:** "Which repository holds your MCP servers?" Choices: a repo they name, "no repo yet", "not sure". If none, offer to start with a local folder.
2. **Targets:** "Which sites or APIs will the MCPs call?" Free text; then ask, per target, whether it is a public page, a signed-in site, or an official API, and whether it is known to be bot-protected.
3. **Coding agent:** "Who opens the PRs?" Choices: "a coding agent", "me", "you (draft only)", "mixed". Note that the bot reviews and drafts; it does not merge.
4. Optional, **live-test risk:** "How careful should live tests be?" Choices: "very careful (default budgets halved)", "standard defaults", "I'll set budgets per site".
Stop asking once you have enough; skip questions already answered.

## 2. Save memories (profile facts only)
- Repo (or "none yet"), target sites/APIs and their type, who opens PRs, live-test risk level, the owner's time zone.
- No secrets, tokens, account ids, or personal data. Never store credentials in memory.

## 3. Create the private working copy
On the owner's computer (or the bot's workspace if they prefer), create a `PLAYBOOK.md` that is theirs to grow:
- Header: owner's project name, date, "private working copy; the public skills are the portable layer; keep them in sync".
- Sections seeded from `mcp-design-build`, `mcp-live-testing`, `mcp-review-grade` (rules summarized, sources linked, not copied).
- Empty sections for: project-specific cases, Prefer-X-when-Y rules, per-site budgets, run log.
- Sync rule: any new rule learned that is generic goes back into the matching skill in the same session.

## 4. Set up the cooldown file
Create `site-cooldowns.json` next to the playbook with `schema: 1` and one entry per target from step 2: no block yet, `not_before` null, budgets at the chosen risk level (see `mcp-live-testing`). Tell the owner where it lives and that every live run reads it first.

## 5. Offer a first task
Offer one, as choices:
- "Review an open MCP PR" (`mcp-review-grade`)
- "Design a new server for <target>" (`mcp-design-build`)
- "Write a live-test plan, without running it" (`mcp-live-testing`)
- "Just look around the repo and summarize"

## If the owner skips or is unsure
- No repo: work in a local folder; ask again when a repo exists.
- Unknown targets: assume bot-protected and use the careful budgets.
- Unknown PR author: assume drafts only, and never merge.
- They want to start right away: save what you have, create the files, and come back to the open questions later.

## Done when
- [ ] Profile facts saved (no secrets)
- [ ] `PLAYBOOK.md` working copy created and its path shared
- [ ] `site-cooldowns.json` created with one entry per target
- [ ] First task offered

## Tone
Short, warm, plain words. Confirm what you saved in one line. Never run a live test or open a PR during setup.

skills.name: mcp-live-testing
skills.description: Use this when about to run, plan, or approve any test of an MCP server that sends real requests to a live site or API.
skills.content:
---
name: mcp-live-testing
description: >-
  Use this when about to run, plan, or approve any test of an MCP server that
  sends real requests to a live site or API.
---
# Polite live testing

Live calls are a scarce, shared resource: every request spends the site's patience and can block every agent behind the same IP. Offline first; live only for what offline cannot prove. Building is covered by `mcp-design-build`; grading by `mcp-review-grade`.

## Sources
- RFC 6585 §4 (429, Retry-After): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
- RFC 9110 §10.2.3 Retry-After, §15.5.4 403, §15.6.4 503: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
- RFC 9309 robots.txt: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309
- Exponential back-off and jitter: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/
- Playwright HAR replay (`route_from_har`): https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-browsercontext

## 1. Offline first
- Run the full suite offline: saved JSON, recorded HTML, HAR replay, fake transports with injected faults.
- A live run is a smoke check of what only live data can show (current site shape, block behavior, real timings). Never a full regression suite.

## 2. Written plan before any run
No plan, no run. Save it with the run notes:
```
Run id / date / tester:
Server + version under test:
Cooldown check: <file> host=<host> not_before=<time> → OK to start? (y/n)
Offline already verified: <list>
Live checks (each: why it needs live data, expected requests):
  L1 … (n)   L2 … (n)
Total expected requests: N  (budget per run: B, used today: U)
Pacing: ≥3 s between calls, one session, no parallel runs
Stop rule: first 403/429/challenge → stop, write cooldown, report
Earliest start / latest end:
```

## 3. Budgets
Method: count the requests each check needs (prime + list + pages + JSON), add 50% margin, and keep the per-run total far below the lowest volume at which you have ever seen a block. Spread runs across the day.
Conservative defaults for a bot-protected site (tighten after any block):
- ≤40 requests per run, ≤15 minutes, ≤2 in flight
- ≤120 requests per day, ≤3 runs per day, runs ≥3 h apart
- ≤1 list/map download and ≤1 prime per process

## 4. Pacing
- ≥3 s between calls (≥4 s for full page loads), jittered.
- One live session per site at a time across all agents: no parallel testers, no overlapping runs. Record start/end times so overlaps are visible.

## 5. Stop on the first block
- 403, 429, or a challenge page (including a challenge body served with HTTP 200) = block. Stop the run; do not retry in-process.
- Honor `Retry-After` (seconds or HTTP-date) when present; it wins over any computed delay.
- Retries only for timeouts/5xx without block markers: full jitter `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base·2^attempt))`, at most 2 attempts.

## 6. Shared cooldown file
One JSON file, readable by every agent and every server process:
```json
{"schema": 1, "hosts": {"example.com": {
  "blocked_first_seen": "ISO-8601", "blocked_last_seen": "ISO-8601",
  "streak": 1, "cooldown_hours": 24, "not_before": "ISO-8601",
  "budget": {"per_run": 40, "per_day": 120, "runs_per_day": 3},
  "used_today": {"date": "YYYY-MM-DD", "requests": 0, "runs": 0},
  "active_run": null}}}
```
Check procedure before any request: (a) read the file; (b) if `now < not_before` → do not run; (c) if `active_run` is set and not stale → do not run; (d) if today's budget cannot cover the plan → do not run; (e) set `active_run`, run, update `used_today`; (f) on a block: `streak += 1`, `cooldown_hours = min(24·2^(streak-1), 72)`, `not_before = last_block + cooldown_hours`; clear `active_run` at the end. Reset `streak` after a clean run.

## 7. Fixtures: capture and scrub
- Capture once, live, under the plan; record URL, status, time, and where each value lives in a manifest. Capture non-200 cases too (404, 403 body, challenge at 200).
- Scrub at capture time with stable placeholders: API keys, URL signatures, bot-manager ids and tokens, bot-manager script paths, cookies/session/CSRF/nonces, analytics ids, IPs, personal emails.
- Scanner allowlists are narrow and tied to a field pattern; never skip a whole folder.
- Prove the scanner works: plant a realistic, high-entropy fake key in a temp copy and confirm the scan fails (low-entropy fakes are often ignored).

## 8. Stopping a run
- Kill the whole process group (`kill -- -<pgid>`), not just the parent script; child processes keep sending requests otherwise.
- Verify with `ps` that no children remain, and check the logs for requests after the stop time.

## 9. Disclose breaches
Any overlap, budget overrun, request after a block or after a stop, or missing cooldown check goes in the run notes: what happened, times, request counts by status, and the cooldown it caused. Never omit it from the summary.

## 10. End-to-end baselines
Record spawn → initialize → first answer, plus per-call timings, cold and warm, with request counts. Compare runs only against baselines measured the same way.

skills.name: mcp-review-grade
skills.description: Use this when reviewing, grading, or re-testing an MCP server pull request and reporting PASS or FAIL.
skills.content:
---
name: mcp-review-grade
description: >-
  Use this when reviewing, grading, or re-testing an MCP server pull request and
  reporting PASS or FAIL.
---
# Review and grade an MCP PR

Trust nothing in the PR body until a file, test, log, or run shows it. Design rules live in `mcp-design-build`; live-run rules in `mcp-live-testing`.

## Sources
- MCP spec: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification
- Writing tools for agents (evals, descriptions): https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
- RFC 6585 / RFC 9110 for block handling: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585 , https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

## 1. Read the PR
Metadata, file list, full diff, CI check runs and failing job logs. Read changed files at the head commit, not at the default branch. Note the head commit in the report. Check CI failures against the base branch: say whether the diff caused them or they were already there.

## 2. Checklist
- **Spec:** current revision; names, schemas, `outputSchema`, deterministic `tools/list`; errors as tool results.
- **Tool design:** ≤10 tools, prefixed, clear descriptions, concise default, size cap, honest annotations.
- **Deadlines:** one deadline reaches launch, prime, lookups, pages, batches; nothing network in the lifespan.
- **Caching:** cache-first, stale-while-revalidate, bounded refresh with per-success writes, corrupt-file quarantine, negative caching.
- **Read-only:** GET by default, guarded clicks, guard tests.
- **Site respect:** pacing, ≤2 in flight, stop on first block, Retry-After, persisted cooldown.
- **Fixtures and secrets:** scrubbed captures, narrow allowlists, scanner proven with a planted fake.
- **Offline tests:** cover each claim; request counts asserted; CI green or failure explained.
- **Docs:** README, agent guide, tool descriptions match behavior.

## 3. Verify each PR claim
Make a table: claim → evidence (file:line, test name, log line, run result) → verified / contradicted / could_not_verify. A claim with no evidence is not verified.

## 4. Site-respect grade
Count requests in the run by type and status (200, 404, 403, 429, challenge, timeout), peak in flight, minimum gap, requests after the first block, requests after the stop. Grade A–F: A = within budget, paced, stopped on first block, cooldown persisted; F = burst, retries into blocks, or traffic after stop.

## 5. Persona eval
Run realistic multi-step tasks as the intended users would ask them. Report counts: correct/no-change (C/N), partial, failed, could_not_verify, not run. Score = C/N ÷ run. Keep held-out tasks.

## 6. Fresh AI, docs-only eval
Give a new agent only the README, agent guide, and tool list with descriptions. Ask it to complete 3–5 tasks. Record where it picked the wrong tool, passed bad input, or misread a status. Each miss is a docs or description fix.

## 7. Report format
```
VERDICT: PASS | FAIL | PARTIAL   (head <commit>, <date time zone>)
Scores: checklist x/9 · persona C/N a, partial b, failed c, CNV d, not run e · docs-only x/y · site respect <grade> (<counts>)
Timings: spawn→init s, first answer s, p50/p95 per tool, cold/warm
Notes: <path to run notes>
Fix list:
 1. <file> — <exact change> — verify: <test or command and expected result>
 2. …
could_not_verify: <item — why — what would verify it>
```
Fix items must be executable by a coding agent with no extra context.

## 8. Automatic FAIL triggers
- A claim in the PR body contradicted by code, a test, or a run.
- A network step outside the call deadline, or work in the lifespan that delays initialization.
- Retrying into a block, a burst refresh, or a cooldown that is lost on restart.
- An unscrubbed secret in a fixture, or a scanner allowlist that skips a whole folder.
- A non-ok status that still carries a number, or `bad_input` for a site failure.
- A live call in CI or in the default test run.

## 9. Honesty rules
- Mark anything not observed as `could_not_verify` with the reason (site blocked, page unfetched, no capture).
- Never re-run live checks to fill gaps without a plan and an expired cooldown (`mcp-live-testing`).
- Disclose your own test breaches in the report.

skills.name: mcp-design-build
skills.description: Use this when designing, building, or changing an MCP server or one of its tools, fetchers, caches, or fixtures.
skills.content:
---
name: mcp-design-build
description: >-
  Use this when designing, building, or changing an MCP server or one of its
  tools, fetchers, caches, or fixtures.
---
# MCP design and build

Build small, read-only, spec-current MCP servers that answer fast, spend few tokens, and treat the sites they read with respect. Live testing is covered by `mcp-live-testing`; reviewing by `mcp-review-grade`.

## Sources (read them, don't copy them)
- MCP spec (current revision, tools, security): https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning and https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification
- MCP Python SDK: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk and https://py.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/
- FastMCP tools: https://gofastmcp.com/servers/tools
- Writing tools for agents: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
- Playwright browser contexts and timeouts: https://playwright.dev/python/docs/browser-contexts and https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-browsertype
- Retry-After and block statuses: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110 and https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
- robots.txt: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309
Check the current spec revision and SDK major version before you start; pin the SDK explicitly (e.g. `>=1.x,<2`) and do SDK major-version ports in their own PR, never inside a feature PR.

## 0. Site recon (before design)
Predict the site's obstacles before writing code. Live runs should only confirm what you predicted. Write `RECON.md` and give each tool area a risk grade. No design, code or live call before it exists.

**Order and budget.**
1. Your own captures and logs: grep saved headers, cookies and bodies for vendor markers.
2. Web archives (raw-mode snapshots and the CDX status history) for robots.txt, terms and sitemaps.
3. Docs: the site's developer or partner programme, government or open datasets, community datasets, vendor docs.
4. Only if the site's cooldown is clear and the daily budget has room: at most 3 polite live GETs (robots.txt, one page, one JSON endpoint), spaced by at least the crawl-delay, from a plain identifiable client with no browser. Save status, headers and cookie names. Stop on the first block.

**Answer each of these with a quote and URL, or mark it `could_not_verify`:**
- Bot vendor, from cookies, headers, script paths and body markers:
  - Akamai: `_abck`, `bm_sz`, `ak_bmsc`, `bm_sv`; an obfuscated first-party script with `?v=…&t=…`; "Access Denied … Reference #".
  - Cloudflare: `cf-ray`, `__cf_bm`, `cf_clearance`, `/cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/`.
  - HUMAN/PerimeterX: `_px*`, `_pxhd`, `_pxvid`.
  - DataDome: `datadome`, Device Check.
  - Imperva: `incap_ses_*`, `visid_incap_*`, `reese84`.
  - Kasada: `x-kpsdk-*`.
  Identify only. Never decode, replay or generate these values.
- Official API, partner or allowlist programme, feeds, sitemaps, public JSON, open datasets: auth, quota, licence, freshness, coverage.
- robots.txt rules and crawl-delay for each path family, and every terms clause on automated access. An Allow is not permission (RFC 9309), and a missing clause is not permission either.
- Auth wall: logged-in data goes through the official OAuth or partner API where one exists; otherwise only user-browser mode with the user's own live session (section 9). Never store, export or replay credentials or cookies.
- Rendering: SSR JSON in the raw HTML (`__NEXT_DATA__`, JSON-LD, inline state), XHR JSON after client JS, or rendered DOM only.
- Known anti-bot behaviours, and how a well-behaved client honours each one: a challenge or 403: stop, close the page and arm the persisted cooldown; a 429: honour Retry-After; score creep with volume: bulk and cache.
  Never solve or evade a challenge, mask automation (stealth flags, UA spoofing), allow a sensor POST, or wait out a challenge or tune timing to get past it.

**Decision ladder.** Pick the highest rung that answers the tool's question:
1. official API;
2. public JSON, feed or open dataset;
3. cached SSR HTML;
4. a browser: an automated, unmasked browser only on green or amber sites; opt-in user-browser mode (section 9) on any grade unless the `red_hard` latch is set;
5. a deep link plus cached or open data with `as_of`. This is the default on red, and always available.

**Risk grade per area** (overall = the worst area used):
- **Green**: official or open source, or no bot manager and no blocks. Build normally.
- **Amber**: bot manager present but no challenges at planned volume, or a third-party dataset with licence or provenance questions. Cache-first, bulk and infrequent; re-grade after any block.
- **Red**: bot manager present and challenges or 403s seen from datacenter or residential IPs, or the path needs a masked browser or sensor POST, or robots/terms disallow it. No automated live access. Choose another source, rung 5 or user-browser mode, and keep old automated code disabled by default.

Re-run recon when you add a tool area, after any block, when vendor markers change, or every 90 days.

## 1. Shape: a small shared kit plus per-site servers
- One shared kit library: response envelope + JSON schema, error types, **site guard** (section 5), request/click guard, redaction, drift helpers, in-memory test client, secret/fixture scanners.
- One server per site, same layout: `server.py` (tools only), a fetch module, `parse.py`, `selectors.py`, `policy.py` (site lists, allowed hosts), `cache.py`, `tests/`, `README.md`, a short agent guide, `requirements.txt`, `run.sh`.
- Servers import the kit; they never copy it. Site-specific lists stay in the server.

## 2. Tool design
- Few tools that match real tasks; consolidate chained steps; at most 10 per server.
- Names: `<site>_<verb>_<noun>`, 1–128 chars from `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`, unique; prefix so they stay distinct next to other servers. `tools/list` order is deterministic and never varies per connection.
- Descriptions are for a new hire: what it returns, when to use it, limits (radius, page size, freshness), and what each non-ok status means for this tool.
- Inputs: a strict JSON Schema (types, enums, bounds, unambiguous names like `zip`, `location_slug`, never `id`). A no-argument tool still declares an empty object schema.
- Output: one envelope on every tool (`status`, `data`, `as_of`, `source`, `hint`), returned as structured content with a JSON text copy and a declared `outputSchema`.
- Token efficiency: high-signal fields, names over opaque ids, `response_format: concise|detailed` (concise by default), pagination/filters, a hard size cap with a truncation note that says how to narrow.
- Annotations: `readOnlyHint`, `openWorldHint`, `idempotentHint` (only if true), `destructiveHint` set honestly. They are hints to clients, not a safety control.
- Errors: input mistakes the model can fix come back as tool execution errors with the valid options; protocol errors only for malformed requests. Statuses are distinct: `ok` (including empty data); `could_not_verify` (site blocked or unreadable); `needs_human` (user-browser mode hit a challenge the user must solve); `needs_extension` (the browser-extension bridge is required but not installed or connected); `bad_input` (caller error only); `error` (our bug or a site shape change). Never emit a number on a non-ok status.
- Every derived number carries its source row and `as_of`. Cross-call state only via explicit handles with a stated lifetime.

## 3. One deadline through every step
- Set one deadline at tool entry. Every awaited step gets `timeout = remaining()`: browser launch, context creation, origin prime, list/map download, each page, each batch, each JSON request.
- Never rely on library defaults: a browser launch default can be minutes long. Pass timeouts explicitly to launch, navigation, and context defaults.
- If time is gone, skip remaining steps and return partial rows marked `could_not_verify`.
- No network work in the server lifespan; it delays initialization. Warm lazily inside the first call, under its deadline.
- Prime at most once per call: a prime that timed out still counts as attempted. The page fetcher owns its own prime.
- Budget every fixed wait (settle, API gap, pacing) into the deadline. If a required wait can't fit, return a clear "warming up, retry" with zero further requests. Never send early, never reload, and never treat our own timeout as a site error that arms a cooldown.
- Wrap every batch in an outer timeout (remaining + small slack) as a backstop for a transport that ignores its own timeout.
- Measure end to end (spawn, initialize, first answer) as well as per call, including a slow cold browser launch.

## 4. Caching
- Cache-first: fresh cache means zero site requests.
- Stale-while-revalidate: answer from stale data now (state its age), refresh after the answer, never inside the call's deadline.
- Bounded refresh: cap records per process, at most 2 in flight with a jittered gap, first request alone, write each success to disk immediately (atomic write), stop on the first block, resume next time from what is still stale.
- Negative caching: "no data" and 404 are results; cache them with a shorter TTL so they are not re-fetched every call.
- Corrupt files (binary, truncated, empty, valid JSON of the wrong shape) are quarantined (renamed aside), logged, and treated as a miss. Never crash; never trust a future timestamp.

## 5. One site guard, not per-path checks
Prefer one shared guard that every outbound request passes through over block checks added to each code path, when a server has more than one way to reach a site (startup warm-up, prime, list, details, pages, background refresh). Per-path checks leave gaps. The guard owns:
- the persisted cooldown check before any request (startup and background work included);
- a cooldown store that fails closed: one validating writer updates the host's entry in place under a single map, with schema keys only and no synonyms; a duplicate host, unknown or synonym key, unparseable time or bad JSON reads as blocked, never as clear; test it;
- response classification for every response, prime included: 403, 429, challenge-at-200, 5xx, timeout. Classify challenges on strong signals (challenge URL or title, vendor container, vendor script plus a small body with no expected page marker), never on one loose phrase; JSON bodies are never challenges; prove it on real full-size captures with the phrases injected;
- arming the cooldown on a block (doubling, capped; challenges longer than 403/429), `max(computed, now + Retry-After)`, and a short cooldown after repeated 5xx, saving the raw status plus a scrubbed, length-capped excerpt of the blocked body so false positives can be diagnosed;
- the `red_hard` latch: set on a hard 403 deny or after repeated blocks (e.g. 4 within 7 days); unlike a cooldown it never expires and only an explicit human command clears it;
- retry policy (never on 403/429/challenge; at most once on timeout/5xx with jitter, and not when Retry-After exceeds the time left);
- concurrency and pacing limits, with a gap of at least max(1 s, Crawl-delay).
In a browser client, browser-originated traffic (subresources, page scripts, a challenge's own POST and reload) counts too. After a block, close the page and abort all further traffic to that site.
Add a test that fails if any module makes a request without the guard, and plant deliberate bypasses to prove the test catches them.

## 6. Read-only safety
- GET by default. Any non-GET is an explicit allow-list entry in `policy.py`.
- No clicks, except behind a guard that checks the label against a refuse list (send, submit, book, pay, purchase, delete, confirm) and a test that scans the source for unguarded clicks.
- Redact secrets and personal data before anything is logged or returned.

## 7. Lessons from bot-protected sites
- A page can return HTTP 200 with a challenge body: detect challenge markers; treat it as a block, not as data.
- A browser client may return a 403 response object rather than raising; a prime that "succeeds" can still be a block. Classify responses, don't rely on exceptions.
- Unnamed or retired rows may return 404 rather than an empty 200: record the real per-status behavior from captures.
- Titles and h1s can be generic on every page; the data often lives in embedded JSON. Prove the parser on a capture before shipping.
- The browser launch leaked outside the deadline; a second prime on timeout doubled the cost; a refresh burst of dozens of parallel requests triggered blocks; an in-memory cooldown reset on restart; a startup warm-up ignored the cooldown. Each has a rule above.
- A bot manager can challenge an automated browser on its very first request from both datacenter and residential IPs. That is a red recon grade: don't keep tuning timing or settle delays to get past it. Switch to an official or open source, cached data plus a deep link, or user-browser mode. Masking automation or letting a challenge script run to completion is evasion, not polite browsing.
- An edge deny (403 "Access Denied") on the first CDP-driven navigation, even in the user's own Chrome, comes before any page script runs, so there is nothing for a human to solve. Set `red_hard`; never answer with warm-ups, referrers, a different profile, header changes or proxies.
- A cooldown entry written outside the expected map, under a synonym key, made readers report the site clear. Hence the fail-closed store in section 5.
- Save the raw body and status of every blocked response; a rendered DOM snapshot taken later can differ from what the site actually sent.

## 8. Tests (offline, in CI)
Fresh, stale, corrupt, unwritable cache dir, block means cooldown written, cooldown honored by a new process and by startup, cooldown store fails closed (duplicate host, synonym key, host outside the map, bad time, bad JSON), a 403 deny sets `red_hard` and only the human clear command unsets it, kill mid-refresh keeps partial writes, deadline exceeded at each step (fake clock, real pacing gaps), blocked prime, Retry-After longer than the default cooldown, repeated 5xx, per-status cases from captures, challenge classifier on real captures and injected phrases, no request bypasses the guard (with planted bypasses), envelope schema on every tool, request counts per scenario via a fake transport and through the real client. Every real miss becomes a regression test. Revert check: undo each fix one at a time; at least one test must fail for each.

## 9. Opt-in user-browser mode
The user's own browsing; allowed on any grade unless `red_hard` is set:
- off by default and enabled explicitly;
- attaches over CDP to the user's running Chrome, localhost only (refuse remote hosts, with no override), with a dedicated `--user-data-dir` profile documented in the README along with the risks of the debugging port;
- opens its own new tab and closes only that tab; never touches the user's other tabs, cookies or storage;
- allowed hosts only, read-only, click guard intact, no stealth;
- every request goes through the site guard: pacing of at least max(1 s, Crawl-delay), a per-call cap, the in-flight limit;
- no startup or background browsing;
- on a challenge it returns `needs_human` ("solve the check in the site tab, then ask again") and stops with no retry or poll; a repeat challenge within the window arms the cooldown;
- a 403 or edge deny sets the `red_hard` latch (not a cooldown to wait out); a 429 arms the cooldown with Retry-After;
- if CDP driving is denied, a passive browser-extension bridge (reads only the responses the page makes on its own, starts no requests, no retries) is the remaining live option; without it return a clear `needs_extension` status plus the deep link and cache;
- the README says live behaviour is `could_not_verify` until a human-present live check passes.
